candidates.reason: The comment discusses specific steps and considerations for implementing I2S, such as using high-quality sound files, proper power supply filtering, and attention to electrical noise. These details align with the topic's description of I2S applications.
candidates.comment: These first few suggestions are extremely important. Use a good quality sound file (play the sound file with your computer...if it sounds crappy on your computer, it will ALWAYS sound crappy with your MCU I2S setup). Load sound file into SRAM before playing. Make use of DMA (assures consistent delivery of the sound file to the amplifier). Those will be the important frontend solutions. Now the backend. Use a high quality I2S amplifier. Make sure your DC blocking capacitors to your speakers are properly matched to the speakers you are using (i.e. 4 ohm vs 8 ohm and at what wattage). Use an I2S amplifier that has high pass filter and clipping capabilities built in (in addition to low THD) like the TAS5760L chip. Follow proper power supply filtering (both at the power supply and at the power inputs to all your ICs) and circuit design (i.e. pay attention to crosstalk and EMI/EMC) to prevent any electrical noise from entering/exiting the audio (i.e. means you can only expect so good of sound quality using prebuilt modules vs a custom 4+ layer properly designed PCB). So in the end you may not have found any solutions on the internet because your problem encompasses more than just 'how to improve sound quality'. When you read datasheets, many of them will provide circuit recommendations that will help their product perform. Many times prebuilt modules don't follow all of those recommendations and therefore won't perform with 'quality' in mind.

candidates.comment: Well I did a similar thing back in the day, but using raw audio and only SD and a r-2r ladder. I got the same results. It boils down to a problem with the SD protocol I think. So whenever I switch sectors in the sd card (read 512 bytes (one sector) and need to read another) the sd_read operation takes 1.5 milliseconds instead of the usually instantaneous speed. This results in an audible jitter in the audio. It occurs regardless if you read 1 bytes or a megabyte in burst mode, so long as that read operation has to cross a sector, ıt takes a solid 1.5 millisecond longer. (doesn't get effected by number of sector switches, maybe how computers can read faster -in burst mode-) I think the propper way to fix this is to have the SD read into a sufficiently large buffer and the I2C peripheral reading from that buffer in non-blocking mode (interrupts maybe? even utilising some hard-wired logic similar to what bitluni does) and only refill the buffer when you have read like %90 of it, and while the SD reads still allow the I2S to keep taking what's left of the buffer (so that the DAC will never have to wait for the SD to read). Not sure if this is how the mp3 library works but they probably read a small amount of data, decompress it then play it and when the section is done, they do it again thus when the total amount of bytes read the next section to be read takes 1.5 milliseconds longer, thus the wierd effect.

candidates.comment: Your two choices (well technically 3) to get audio out of any MCU will be DAC (only so many have those built in), PWM and I2S. With the DAC, you will generally want a precision that matches your audio file. So if you have an 8-bit audio file than the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will work great for you. If you have a 10-bit (or higher) audio file then the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will cause a reduction in your sound quality (think 8-bit audio like Nintendo games when Nintendo first came out...don't expect MP3 jamming music). Normally with a DAC you will want 12-bits or higher for at least semi-decent audio (which then usually means an external DAC and an additional IC since you still need an amplifier). PWM is worse because it takes a lot of overhead to convert your sound file into a PWM signal that will then be smoothed to an analog output via filtering (which also reduces sound quality). PWM sound is basically if you have no other choice and you are ok with crappy sound. Now I2S reigns supreme for this because it is digital data and not analog (which is what your sound file comes in). In addition if you get a proper I2S amplifier (a TAS5760L can do 20W @ 12V mono or 10W @ 12V stereo), you can send the data directly out (via DMA - for proper sound quality you will want to use DMA) to the amplifier and the amplifier will take care of converting the digital signal to an amplified analog audio signal. In addition, the TAS5760L has an I2C interface that allows you to adjust things like gain, volume, clipping...even tells you if a fault has occurred with some faults being fully recoverable.

I want to add a little to the whole sampling rate debate. 44.1khz is all you need. It is in fact enough to PERFECTLY represent an audio signal ranging between 0Hz and 20khz. You do not need more. It is completely wasted to add more. Reason: you only need twice as many sampling points as the highest frequency you want to digitise. The rest can be mathematically interpolated. 
Higher Bit Depth can be usefull for higher volumes. Also it gives more freedom when mastering the song. However, as a listener you only need a certain amount of dynamic range. 16Bit is completely fine. You may argue for 24Bit but anything above is only useful at volumes that would completely destroy your ears.

candidates.reason: The comment discusses the options for audio output from an MCU, including I2S, and explains its advantages over DAC and PWM. Although it does not specifically mention pin selection or ESP32's I2S peripherals, it is strongly related to the topic as it focuses on the same peripheral (I2S) and its application in achieving high-quality audio output.
candidates.comment: Your two choices (well technically 3) to get audio out of any MCU will be DAC (only so many have those built in), PWM and I2S. With the DAC, you will generally want a precision that matches your audio file. So if you have an 8-bit audio file than the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will work great for you. If you have a 10-bit (or higher) audio file then the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will cause a reduction in your sound quality (think 8-bit audio like Nintendo games when Nintendo first came out...don't expect MP3 jamming music). Normally with a DAC you will want 12-bits or higher for at least semi-decent audio (which then usually means an external DAC and an additional IC since you still need an amplifier). PWM is worse because it takes a lot of overhead to convert your sound file into a PWM signal that will then be smoothed to an analog output via filtering (which also reduces sound quality). PWM sound is basically if you have no other choice and you are ok with crappy sound. Now I2S reigns supreme for this because it is digital data and not analog (which is what your sound file comes in). In addition if you get a proper I2S amplifier (a TAS5760L can do 20W @ 12V mono or 10W @ 12V stereo), you can send the data directly out (via DMA - for proper sound quality you will want to use DMA) to the amplifier and the amplifier will take care of converting the digital signal to an amplified analog audio signal. In addition, the TAS5760L has an I2C interface that allows you to adjust things like gain, volume, clipping...even tells you if a fault has occurred with some faults being fully recoverable.

candidates.reason: The comment discusses I2S peripherals on ESP32 (pin selection), amplifier choices, and circuit design considerations, directly aligning with the topic's exploration of I2S peripherals and pin selection.
candidates.comment: These first few suggestions are extremely important. Use a good quality sound file (play the sound file with your computer...if it sounds crappy on your computer, it will ALWAYS sound crappy with your MCU I2S setup). Load sound file into SRAM before playing. Make use of DMA (assures consistent delivery of the sound file to the amplifier). Those will be the important frontend solutions. Now the backend. Use a high quality I2S amplifier. Make sure your DC blocking capacitors to your speakers are properly matched to the speakers you are using (i.e. 4 ohm vs 8 ohm and at what wattage). Use an I2S amplifier that has high pass filter and clipping capabilities built in (in addition to low THD) like the TAS5760L chip. Follow proper power supply filtering (both at the power supply and at the power inputs to all your ICs) and circuit design (i.e. pay attention to crosstalk and EMI/EMC) to prevent any electrical noise from entering/exiting the audio (i.e. means you can only expect so good of sound quality using prebuilt modules vs a custom 4+ layer properly designed PCB). So in the end you may not have found any solutions on the internet because your problem encompasses more than just 'how to improve sound quality'. When you read datasheets, many of them will provide circuit recommendations that will help their product perform. Many times prebuilt modules don't follow all of those recommendations and therefore won't perform with 'quality' in mind.

candidates.comment: Well I did a similar thing back in the day, but using raw audio and only SD and a r-2r ladder. I got the same results. It boils down to a problem with the SD protocol I think. So whenever I switch sectors in the sd card (read 512 bytes (one sector) and need to read another) the sd_read operation takes 1.5 milliseconds instead of the usually instantaneous speed. This results in an audible jitter in the audio. It occurs regardless if you read 1 bytes or a megabyte in burst mode, so long as that read operation has to cross a sector, ıt takes a solid 1.5 millisecond longer. (doesn't get effected by number of sector switches, maybe how computers can read faster -in burst mode-) I think the propper way to fix this is to have the SD read into a sufficiently large buffer and the I2C peripheral reading from that buffer in non-blocking mode (interrupts maybe? even utilising some hard-wired logic similar to what bitluni does) and only refill the buffer when you have read like %90 of it, and while the SD reads still allow the I2S to keep taking what's left of the buffer (so that the DAC will never have to wait for the SD to read). Not sure if this is how the mp3 library works but they probably read a small amount of data, decompress it then play it and when the section is done, they do it again thus when the total amount of bytes read the next section to be read takes 1.5 milliseconds longer, thus the wierd effect.

candidates.reason: The comment discusses sampling frequency and Nyquist theorem, which are not related to I2S peripherals or pin selection on ESP32.
candidates.comment: It's important to note that while greater sampling frequency does increase quality, any sampling frequency above 40 kHz makes irrelevant increase to the human hearing. Because, according do the Nyquist theorem, to perfectly reconstruct a analog signal you need a sampling frequency at least double the analysed signal. Thus we need only 40kHz, as the human hearing only goes to about 20kHz (and that's in very young children, because you'd be lucky to have this hearing past your adolescence). Also speakers are almost always limited to playing till this frequency, so even if you say that frequencies above 20kHz do somehow contribute to sound quality, your speakers won't even play it.

candidates.reason: The comment discusses the same settings (DAC, PWM, I2S), parameters (precision, sound quality) and goals (getting audio out of an MCU) described by the topic, with a clear focus on I2S communication setup.
candidates.comment: Your two choices (well technically 3) to get audio out of any MCU will be DAC (only so many have those built in), PWM and I2S. With the DAC, you will generally want a precision that matches your audio file. So if you have an 8-bit audio file than the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will work great for you. If you have a 10-bit (or higher) audio file then the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will cause a reduction in your sound quality (think 8-bit audio like Nintendo games when Nintendo first came out...don't expect MP3 jamming music). Normally with a DAC you will want 12-bits or higher for at least semi-decent audio (which then usually means an external DAC and an additional IC since you still need an amplifier). PWM is worse because it takes a lot of overhead to convert your sound file into a PWM signal that will then be smoothed to an analog output via filtering (which also reduces sound quality). PWM sound is basically if you have no other choice and you are ok with crappy sound. Now I2S reigns supreme for this because it is digital data and not analog (which is what your sound file comes in). In addition if you get a proper I2S amplifier (a TAS5760L can do 20W @ 12V mono or 10W @ 12V stereo), you can send the data directly out (via DMA - for proper sound quality you will want to use DMA) to the amplifier and the amplifier will take care of converting the digital signal to an amplified analog audio signal. In addition, the TAS5760L has an I2C interface that allows you to adjust things like gain, volume, clipping...even tells you if a fault has occurred with some faults being fully recoverable.

candidates.reason: The comment directly discusses initializing and starting I2S communication on the ESP32, mentioning specific steps such as loading sound files into SRAM, using DMA for consistent delivery, and setting up proper power supply filtering. The topic's focus on initialization and setup is also echoed in the comment's emphasis on circuit design and component selection.
candidates.comment: These first few suggestions are extremely important. Use a good quality sound file (play the sound file with your computer...if it sounds crappy on your computer, it will ALWAYS sound crappy with your MCU I2S setup). Load sound file into SRAM before playing. Make use of DMA (assures consistent delivery of the sound file to the amplifier). Those will be the important frontend solutions. Now the backend. Use a high quality I2S amplifier. Make sure your DC blocking capacitors to your speakers are properly matched to the speakers you are using (i.e. 4 ohm vs 8 ohm and at what wattage). Use an I2S amplifier that has high pass filter and clipping capabilities built in (in addition to low THD) like the TAS5760L chip. Follow proper power supply filtering (both at the power supply and at the power inputs to all your ICs) and circuit design (i.e. pay attention to crosstalk and EMI/EMC) to prevent any electrical noise from entering/exiting the audio (i.e. means you can only expect so good of sound quality using prebuilt modules vs a custom 4+ layer properly designed PCB). So in the end you may not have found any solutions on the internet because your problem encompasses more than just 'how to improve sound quality'. When you read datasheets, many of them will provide circuit recommendations that will help their product perform. Many times prebuilt modules don't follow all of those recommendations and therefore won't perform with 'quality' in mind.

candidates.comment: Your two choices (well technically 3) to get audio out of any MCU will be DAC (only so many have those built in), PWM and I2S. With the DAC, you will generally want a precision that matches your audio file. So if you have an 8-bit audio file than the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will work great for you. If you have a 10-bit (or higher) audio file then the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will cause a reduction in your sound quality (think 8-bit audio like Nintendo games when Nintendo first came out...don't expect MP3 jamming music). Normally with a DAC you will want 12-bits or higher for at least semi-decent audio (which then usually means an external DAC and an additional IC since you still need an amplifier). PWM is worse because it takes a lot of overhead to convert your sound file into a PWM signal that will then be smoothed to an analog output via filtering (which also reduces sound quality). PWM sound is basically if you have no other choice and you are ok with crappy sound. Now I2S reigns supreme for this because it is digital data and not analog (which is what your sound file comes in). In addition if you get a proper I2S amplifier (a TAS5760L can do 20W @ 12V mono or 10W @ 12V stereo), you can send the data directly out (via DMA - for proper sound quality you will want to use DMA) to the amplifier and the amplifier will take care of converting the digital signal to an amplified analog audio signal. In addition, the TAS5760L has an I2C interface that allows you to adjust things like gain, volume, clipping...even tells you if a fault has occurred with some faults being fully recoverable.

candidates.comment: These first few suggestions are extremely important. Use a good quality sound file (play the sound file with your computer...if it sounds crappy on your computer, it will ALWAYS sound crappy with your MCU I2S setup). Load sound file into SRAM before playing. Make use of DMA (assures consistent delivery of the sound file to the amplifier). Those will be the important frontend solutions. Now the backend. Use a high quality I2S amplifier. Make sure your DC blocking capacitors to your speakers are properly matched to the speakers you are using (i.e. 4 ohm vs 8 ohm and at what wattage). Use an I2S amplifier that has high pass filter and clipping capabilities built in (in addition to low THD) like the TAS5760L chip. Follow proper power supply filtering (both at the power supply and at the power inputs to all your ICs) and circuit design (i.e. pay attention to crosstalk and EMI/EMC) to prevent any electrical noise from entering/exiting the audio (i.e. means you can only expect so good of sound quality using prebuilt modules vs a custom 4+ layer properly designed PCB). So in the end you may not have found any solutions on the internet because your problem encompasses more than just 'how to improve sound quality'. When you read datasheets, many of them will provide circuit recommendations that will help their product perform. Many times prebuilt modules don't follow all of those recommendations and therefore won't perform with 'quality' in mind.

It is completely wasted to add more. Reason: you only need twice as many sampling points as the highest frequency you want to digitise. The rest can be mathematically interpolated. 
Higher Bit Depth can be usefull for higher volumes. Also it gives more freedom when mastering the song. However, as a listener you only need a certain amount of dynamic range. 16Bit is completely fine. You may argue for 24Bit but anything above is only useful at volumes that would completely destroy your ears.

candidates.comment: Well I did a similar thing back in the day, but using raw audio and only SD and a r-2r ladder. I got the same results. It boils down to a problem with the SD protocol I think. So whenever I switch sectors in the sd card (read 512 bytes (one sector) and need to read another) the sd_read operation takes 1.5 milliseconds instead of the usually instantaneous speed. This results in an audible jitter in the audio. It occurs regardless if you read 1 bytes or a megabyte in burst mode, so long as that read operation has to cross a sector, ıt takes a solid 1.5 millisecond longer. (doesn't get effected by number of sector switches, maybe how computers can read faster -in burst mode-) I think the propper way to fix this is to have the SD read into a sufficiently large buffer and the I2C peripheral reading from that buffer in non-blocking mode (interrupts maybe? even utilising some hard-wired logic similar to what bitluni does) and only refill the buffer when you have read like %90 of it, and while the SD reads still allow the I2S to keep taking what's left of the buffer (so that the DAC will never have to wait for the SD to read). Not sure if this is how the mp3 library works but they probably read a small amount of data, decompress it then play it and when the section is done, they do it again thus when the total amount of bytes read the next section to be read takes 1.5 milliseconds longer, thus the wierd effect.

candidates.comment: It's important to note that while greater sampling frequency does increase quality, any sampling frequency above 40 kHz makes irrelevant increase to the human hearing. Because, according do the Nyquist theorem, to perfectly reconstruct a analog signal you need a sampling frequency at least double the analysed signal. Thus we need only 40kHz, as the human hearing only goes to about 20kHz (and that's in very young children, because you'd be lucky to have this hearing past your adolescence). Also speakers are almost always limited to playing till this frequency, so even if you say that frequencies above 20kHz do somehow contribute to sound quality, your speakers won't even play it.

candidates.reason: The comment directly discusses the same topics mentioned in the topic description, such as using a high-quality I2S amplifier, DC blocking capacitors, and proper power supply filtering to improve sound quality. The commenter also mentions circuit design considerations like crosstalk and EMI/EMC, which are all related to the frequency adjustment aspect of the topic.
candidates.comment: These first few suggestions are extremely important. Use a good quality sound file (play the sound file with your computer...if it sounds crappy on your computer, it will ALWAYS sound crappy with your MCU I2S setup). Load sound file into SRAM before playing. Make use of DMA (assures consistent delivery of the sound file to the amplifier). Those will be the important frontend solutions. Now the backend. Use a high quality I2S amplifier. Make sure your DC blocking capacitors to your speakers are properly matched to the speakers you are using (i.e. 4 ohm vs 8 ohm and at what wattage). Use an I2S amplifier that has high pass filter and clipping capabilities built in (in addition to low THD) like the TAS5760L chip. Follow proper power supply filtering (both at the power supply and at the power inputs to all your ICs) and circuit design (i.e. pay attention to crosstalk and EMI/EMC) to prevent any electrical noise from entering/exiting the audio (i.e. means you can only expect so good of sound quality using prebuilt modules vs a custom 4+ layer properly designed PCB). So in the end you may not have found any solutions on the internet because your problem encompasses more than just 'how to improve sound quality'. When you read datasheets, many of them will provide circuit recommendations that will help their product perform. Many times prebuilt modules don't follow all of those recommendations and therefore won't perform with 'quality' in mind.

candidates.comment: Well I did a similar thing back in the day, but using raw audio and only SD and a r-2r ladder. I got the same results. It boils down to a problem with the SD protocol I think. So whenever I switch sectors in the sd card (read 512 bytes (one sector) and need to read another) the sd_read operation takes 1.5 milliseconds instead of the usually instantaneous speed. This results in an audible jitter in the audio. It occurs regardless if you read 1 bytes or a megabyte in burst mode, so long as that read operation has to cross a sector, ıt takes a solid 1.5 millisecond longer. (doesn't get effected by number of sector switches, maybe how computers can read faster -in burst mode-) I think the propper way to fix this is to have the SD read into a sufficiently large buffer and the I2C peripheral reading from that buffer in non-blocking mode (interrupts maybe? even utilising some hard-wired logic similar to what bitluni does) and only refill the buffer when you have read like %90 of it, and while the SD reads still allow the I2S to keep taking what's left of the buffer (so that the DAC will never have to wait for the SD to read). Not sure if this is how the mp3 library works but they probably read a small amount of data, decompress it then play it and when the section is done, they do it again thus when the total amount of bytes read the next section to be read takes 1.5 milliseconds longer, thus the wierd effect.

candidates.reason: The comment directly discusses the frequency adjustment of I2S communication interface, specifically mentioning sampling frequency, Nyquist theorem, and human hearing range, which is strongly related to the topic's description about adjusting the frequency of I2S.
candidates.comment: It's important to note that while greater sampling frequency does increase quality, any sampling frequency above 40 kHz makes irrelevant increase to the human hearing. Because, according do the Nyquist theorem, to perfectly reconstruct a analog signal you need a sampling frequency at least double the analysed signal. candidates.reason: The comment discusses I2S communication interface and its frequency adjustment, directly referencing the topic's description. The comment also mentions I2S amplifier TAS5760L and DMA for proper sound quality, showing strong overlap with the topic.
candidates.comment: Your two choices (well technically 3) to get audio out of any MCU will be DAC (only so many have those built in), PWM and I2S. With the DAC, you will generally want a precision that matches your audio file. So if you have an 8-bit audio file than the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will work great for you. If you have a 10-bit (or higher) audio file then the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will cause a reduction in your sound quality (think 8-bit audio like Nintendo games when Nintendo first came out...don't expect MP3 jamming music). Normally with a DAC you will want 12-bits or higher for at least semi-decent audio (which then usually means an external DAC and an additional IC since you still need an amplifier). PWM is worse because it takes a lot of overhead to convert your sound file into a PWM signal that will then be smoothed to an analog output via filtering (which also reduces sound quality). PWM sound is basically if you have no other choice and you are ok with crappy sound. Now I2S reigns supreme for this because it is digital data and not analog (which is what your sound file comes in). In addition if you get a proper I2S amplifier (a TAS5760L can do 20W @ 12V mono or 10W @ 12V stereo), you can send the data directly out (via DMA - for proper sound quality you will want to use DMA) to the amplifier and the amplifier will take care of converting the digital signal to an amplified analog audio signal. In addition, the TAS5760L has an I2C interface that allows you to adjust things like gain, volume, clipping...even tells you if a fault has occurred with some faults being fully recoverable.

candidates.comment: Your two choices (well technically 3) to get audio out of any MCU will be DAC (only so many have those built in), PWM and I2S. With the DAC, you will generally want a precision that matches your audio file. So if you have an 8-bit audio file than the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will work great for you. If you have a 10-bit (or higher) audio file then the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will cause a reduction in your sound quality (think 8-bit audio like Nintendo games when Nintendo first came out...don't expect MP3 jamming music). Normally with a DAC you will want 12-bits or higher for at least semi-decent audio (which then usually means an external DAC and an additional IC since you still need an amplifier). PWM is worse because it takes a lot of overhead to convert your sound file into a PWM signal that will then be smoothed to an analog output via filtering (which also reduces sound quality). PWM sound is basically if you have no other choice and you are ok with crappy sound. Now I2S reigns supreme for this because it is digital data and not analog (which is what your sound file comes in). In addition if you get a proper I2S amplifier (a TAS5760L can do 20W @ 12V mono or 10W @ 12V stereo), you can send the data directly out (via DMA - for proper sound quality you will want to use DMA) to the amplifier and the amplifier will take care of converting the digital signal to an amplified analog audio signal. In addition, the TAS5760L has an I2C interface that allows you to adjust things like gain, volume, clipping...even tells you if a fault has occurred with some faults being fully recoverable.

candidates.reason: The comment directly discusses the use of I2S with an amplifier and microSD card to play audio, mentioning specific details like SRAM, DMA, DC blocking capacitors, and power supply filtering, which strongly relate to the topic.
candidates.comment: These first few suggestions are extremely important. Use a good quality sound file (play the sound file with your computer...if it sounds crappy on your computer, it will ALWAYS sound crappy with your MCU I2S setup). Load sound file into SRAM before playing. Make use of DMA (assures consistent delivery of the sound file to the amplifier). Those will be the important frontend solutions. Now the backend. Use a high quality I2S amplifier. Make sure your DC blocking capacitors to your speakers are properly matched to the speakers you are using (i.e. 4 ohm vs 8 ohm and at what wattage). Use an I2S amplifier that has high pass filter and clipping capabilities built in (in addition to low THD) like the TAS5760L chip. Follow proper power supply filtering (both at the power supply and at the power inputs to all your ICs) and circuit design (i.e. pay attention to crosstalk and EMI/EMC) to prevent any electrical noise from entering/exiting the audio (i.e. means you can only expect so good of sound quality using prebuilt modules vs a custom 4+ layer properly designed PCB). So in the end you may not have found any solutions on the internet because your problem encompasses more than just 'how to improve sound quality'. When you read datasheets, many of them will provide circuit recommendations that will help their product perform. Many times prebuilt modules don't follow all of those recommendations and therefore won't perform with 'quality' in mind.

candidates.comment: Well I did a similar thing back in the day, but using raw audio and only SD and a r-2r ladder. I got the same results. It boils down to a problem with the SD protocol I think. So whenever I switch sectors in the sd card (read 512 bytes (one sector) and need to read another) the sd_read operation takes 1.5 milliseconds instead of the usually instantaneous speed. This results in an audible jitter in the audio. It occurs regardless if you read 1 bytes or a megabyte in burst mode, so long as that read operation has to cross a sector, ıt takes a solid 1.5 millisecond longer. (doesn't get effected by number of sector switches, maybe how computers can read faster -in burst mode-) I think the propper way to fix this is to have the SD read into a sufficiently large buffer and the I2C peripheral reading from that buffer in non-blocking mode (interrupts maybe? even utilising some hard-wired logic similar to what bitluni does) and only refill the buffer when you have read like %90 of it, and while the SD reads still allow the I2S to keep taking what's left of the buffer (so that the DAC will never have to wait for the SD to read). Not sure if this is how the mp3 library works but they probably read a small amount of data, decompress it then play it and when the section is done, they do it again thus when the total amount of bytes read the next section to be read takes 1.5 milliseconds longer, thus the wierd effect.

I want to add a little to the whole sampling rate debate. 44.1khz is all you need. It is in fact enough to PERFECTLY represent an audio signal ranging between 0Hz and 20khz. You do not need more. It is completely wasted to add more. Reason: you only need twice as many sampling points as the highest frequency you want to digitise. The rest can be mathematically interpolated. 
Higher Bit Depth can be usefull for higher volumes. Also it gives more freedom when mastering the song. However, as a listener you only need a certain amount of dynamic range. 16Bit is completely fine. You may argue for 24Bit but anything above is only useful at volumes that would completely destroy your ears.

candidates.comment: It's important to note that while greater sampling frequency does increase quality, any sampling frequency above 40 kHz makes irrelevant increase to the human hearing. Because, according do the Nyquist theorem, to perfectly reconstruct a analog signal you need a sampling frequency at least double the analysed signal. Thus we need only 40kHz, as the human hearing only goes to about 20kHz (and that's in very young children, because you'd be lucky to have this hearing past your adolescence). Also speakers are almost always limited to playing till this frequency, so even if you say that frequencies above 20kHz do somehow contribute to sound quality, your speakers won't even play it.

candidates.reason: The comment directly discusses the same steps and settings described by the topic, including suggestions for improving sound quality (e.g. using a high-quality amplifier, properly matched DC blocking capacitors), circuit design considerations (e.g. power supply filtering, crosstalk prevention) and reading datasheets to improve product performance.
candidates.comment: These first few suggestions are extremely important. Use a good quality sound file (play the sound file with your computer...if it sounds crappy on your computer, it will ALWAYS sound crappy with your MCU I2S setup). Load sound file into SRAM before playing. Make use of DMA (assures consistent delivery of the sound file to the amplifier). Those will be the important frontend solutions. Now the backend. Use a high quality I2S amplifier. Make sure your DC blocking capacitors to your speakers are properly matched to the speakers you are using (i.e. 4 ohm vs 8 ohm and at what wattage). Use an I2S amplifier that has high pass filter and clipping capabilities built in (in addition to low THD) like the TAS5760L chip. Follow proper power supply filtering (both at the power supply and at the power inputs to all your ICs) and circuit design (i.e. pay attention to crosstalk and EMI/EMC) to prevent any electrical noise from entering/exiting the audio (i.e. means you can only expect so good of sound quality using prebuilt modules vs a custom 4+ layer properly designed PCB). So in the end you may not have found any solutions on the internet because your problem encompasses more than just 'how to improve sound quality'. When you read datasheets, many of them will provide circuit recommendations that will help their product perform. Many times prebuilt modules don't follow all of those recommendations and therefore won't perform with 'quality' in mind.

candidates.reason: The comment discusses specific details on getting audio out of an MCU (DAC, PWM, I2S), which directly relates to the topic 'Conclusion and Next Steps' with its focus on suggestions for further learning.
candidates.comment: Your two choices (well technically 3) to get audio out of any MCU will be DAC (only so many have those built in), PWM and I2S. With the DAC, you will generally want a precision that matches your audio file. So if you have an 8-bit audio file than the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will work great for you. If you have a 10-bit (or higher) audio file then the 8-bit DAC on the ESP32 will cause a reduction in your sound quality (think 8-bit audio like Nintendo games when Nintendo first came out...don't expect MP3 jamming music). Normally with a DAC you will want 12-bits or higher for at least semi-decent audio (which then usually means an external DAC and an additional IC since you still need an amplifier). PWM is worse because it takes a lot of overhead to convert your sound file into a PWM signal that will then be smoothed to an analog output via filtering (which also reduces sound quality). PWM sound is basically if you have no other choice and you are ok with crappy sound. Now I2S reigns supreme for this because it is digital data and not analog (which is what your sound file comes in). In addition if you get a proper I2S amplifier (a TAS5760L can do 20W @ 12V mono or 10W @ 12V stereo), you can send the data directly out (via DMA - for proper sound quality you will want to use DMA) to the amplifier and the amplifier will take care of converting the digital signal to an amplified analog audio signal. In addition, the TAS5760L has an I2C interface that allows you to adjust things like gain, volume, clipping...even tells you if a fault has occurred with some faults being fully recoverable.
